draft_text:
A sculpture of an artist's head sits on the facade of a former brewery in Neukölln. Bees crawl in and out through its nostrils and mouth. The figure is 3D-printed from cornstarch — biodegradable, edible, a temporary host for another species' architecture. This is Simon Faithfull's *Biotope no.1: Bienenstock*, and it tells you almost everything you need to know about where the lecture performances at KINDL on 18 April are coming from: the porous boundary between the human body and everything else that lives.

Faithfull, born 1966 in Ipsden, UK, now Berlin-based, has spent decades making work that positions the human figure as an awkward, frequently absurd presence within larger ecological systems. His solo exhibition *Earth-ling*, running at KINDL's M1 VideoSpace through late July, gathers videos, photographs and sculptures around this central preoccupation — the body encountering what the exhibition materials call "the living fabric of this planet." [~The phrase is drawn directly from KINDL's own exhibition text|only source available for this description; no independent reviews of the show have surfaced yet~]. His lecture performance, *Explaining Taxonomy to a Bird*, places itself squarely in the tradition of the artist talk that refuses to simply explain. The title alone — that deadpan image of a human standing before a bird, attempting to communicate the classificatory systems we have invented to organise nature — carries a comic futility that runs through much of Faithfull's practice, from his early GPS drawings made by walking straight lines across landscapes to his later Antarctic expeditions filmed with a lo-fi digital intimacy.

Paired with Faithfull is Gabriella Hirst, an Australian artist and writer now also based in Berlin, whose work traces the entanglements of care, control and colonial history through moving image, performance, installation and — notably — gardening. Her lecture performance, *Ambergris*, takes its name from the waxy, foul-then-fragrant substance produced in the digestive systems of sperm whales, historically prized by perfumers and still the subject of peculiar legal and ethical dispute. Ambergris is a substance that collapses categories: animal waste or luxury commodity, ocean debris or olfactory treasure. It is precisely the kind of material through which Hirst works — where plant taxonomies meet landscape painting, where art conservation intersects with nuclear history, where the archival meets the anecdotal.

Hirst's trajectory has been conspicuously international. A recipient of the 2020 ACMI/Ian Potter Moving Image Commission, she has held residencies at Villa Romana in Florence, Cité Internationale des Arts in Paris, ZKU in Berlin, Cove Park in Scotland, and Delfina Foundation in London. Her recent exhibitions include Kunsthalle Osnabrück and the Sainsbury Centre; her lecture performances and film screenings have appeared at the Dia Art Foundation, CARA in New York, and the Wende Museum in Los Angeles. Her artist book *Battlefield* launched at Printed Matter's NY Art Book Fair in 2024. [~This biographical detail is well-documented across multiple institutional sources — Delfina Foundation, KINDL, and her own professional listings all converge~]. At Delfina, she was researching stillness, preservation, 'Keep Calm and Carry On' rhetoric, wax museums and death masks — a constellation that suggests her work is consistently drawn to the ways cultures embalm, classify and freeze the living world into manageable forms.

The double bill sits within KINDL's broader spring programme, which includes Hirst's group exhibition *An Intimacy with Strangers* and Faithfull's *Earth-ling*, both of which opened on 21 March. The conversation following the performances will be moderated by Jessica Ullrich, an art historian based in Nuremberg whose writing focuses on the intersection of art and animal studies — a fitting interlocutor for two artists whose work keeps circling the question of how humans narrate their relationship to non-human life.

The lecture performance as a format has become so prevalent in contemporary art that it risks its own kind of banality — the artist stands at a lectern, clicks through slides, tells a story that blurs documentation and fiction, and the audience nods along in a register somewhere between TED talk and theatre. KINDL itself has programmed several this spring: Ana Prvački's *How Sex Keeps Us from Floating Away* and Alexandra Grant's *The Storm is Around You Not in You* both featured in the *Iliggocene – The Age of Dizziness* programme in March. [~This is drawn from KINDL's own event archive; no external reviews of these individual performances have been located~]. The format proliferates because it solves a practical problem — it is cheap, portable, and allows artists to present research-based practices without fabricating large-scale installations — but also because it occupies an epistemological grey zone that suits the current moment. It is not quite a talk, not quite a show. It lets the artist be simultaneously expert and unreliable narrator.

What makes this particular pairing interesting is the way both artists approach the same fundamental territory — the violence and absurdity of human classificatory systems imposed on the non-human world — through markedly different registers. Faithfull tends toward the deadpan, the embodied, the slightly slapstick: a body in a landscape doing something faintly ridiculous with great seriousness. Hirst works through layered archival storytelling, pulling threads between colonial botanical gardens and nuclear test sites, between perfume and whale intestines. One performs taxonomy's failure as physical comedy; the other narrates it as a slow-burning historical horror story.

KINDL itself matters as a context. The former Berliner Kindl brewery in Neukölln — its expressionist tower and 20-metre-high boiler house converted into exhibition spaces under curator Kathrin Becker's direction — is a building that already performs a kind of taxonomic confusion: industrial heritage repurposed as art institution, a site where the ghost of mass production haunts the singularity of contemporary art objects. The Maschinenhaus, the Sudhaus, the Kesselhaus — these are rooms named for processes of heating, brewing, fermenting. Organic transformation as architectural memory. It is not a neutral white cube, and work shown there inevitably enters into dialogue with the building's own story of substances processed and changed.

The event is free, in English, at 15:00 on a Saturday afternoon. There is something worth noting in this accessibility — a double lecture performance followed by a moderated conversation in a former brewery in Neukölln, no ticket price, no velvet rope. Berlin still offers this, even as the city's institutional landscape tightens and gallery funding grows more precarious. Whether the format can sustain genuine criticality or becomes another soft-power vehicle for institutional programming is a question that applies to every lecture performance everywhere. But when two artists with this much specificity in their research — whale vomit, bee-colonised self-portraits, the absurdity of explaining taxonomy to a creature that preceded it — stand in front of an audience and speak, the format still has the capacity to do what a wall text cannot. It can hesitate. It can digress. It can look at its own categories and find them, briefly, laughable.
critique_assessment: Strong essay with genuine insight and a clear point of view, but needs targeted fixes: some unverifiable biographical claims, one critical factual issue with the event time, a slightly bloated CV paragraph, and a "Whether..." construction that needs killing.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 1 — 'A sculpture of an artist's head sits on the facade... Simon Faithfull's *Biotope no.1: Bienenstock*'
critique_issues.fix: This artwork description is not verifiable from any of the provided source material. It reads like a real piece, and Faithfull does work in this vein, but the specific title, the cornstarch detail, the nostril-and-mouth bee entry — none of this can be confirmed here. Either source it or soften the claim. I'll add a confidence marker in the revision.
Birth year and birthplace are not in the source material. This has hallucination risk. Remove the specific birth year and birthplace — say 'British, now Berlin-based' and leave it clean.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 2 — 'his early GPS drawings made by walking straight lines across landscapes to his later Antarctic expeditions filmed with a lo-fi digital intimacy'
critique_issues.fix: These biographical details about GPS drawings and Antarctic expeditions are plausible for Faithfull but unverifiable from provided sources. Add a confidence marker.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 4 — Hirst's extensive CV (ACMI commission, Villa Romana, Cité Internationale des Arts, etc.)
critique_issues.fix: While the essay's own confidence marker says this is well-documented, none of these specifics appear in the provided source material. The 2020 date for the ACMI commission, the specific residency list, Printed Matter's NY Art Book Fair 2024 — all unverifiable here. The paragraph also reads like a CV dump that kills the essay's momentum. Trim drastically; keep only what serves the argument.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5 — 'both of which opened on 21 March'
critique_issues.fix: The source material shows the Iliggocene programme was on 22.3, but doesn't explicitly confirm the exhibitions opened on 21 March. The date is plausible but unverifiable. Soften to 'opened in March.'
Kathrin Becker is not mentioned in the provided source material. Could be accurate but unverifiable here. Remove the specific name or add a marker.

The source material says the date is 18 April 2026. April 18, 2026 is a Saturday — that checks out. But the time 15:00 is not stated anywhere in the sources. Don't invent a time. Remove it or flag it.

This is the essay's dead zone. After three paragraphs of genuinely engaging writing, we hit a wall of institutional name-dropping (Villa Romana, Cité Internationale des Arts, ZKU, Cove Park, Delfina, Kunsthalle Osnabrück, Sainsbury Centre, Dia, CARA, Wende Museum, Printed Matter). It reads like a grant application. The Delfina research detail at the end is the only part that earns its place. Cut the residency list, keep the Delfina research, and fold the rest into a single sentence.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6 — 'the audience nods along in a register somewhere between TED talk and theatre'
critique_issues.fix: This is good observation but 'TED talk' as a reference point is becoming its own cliché in art criticism. It's fine — barely — but worth noting.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 9 — 'Whether the format can sustain genuine criticality or becomes another soft-power vehicle...'
critique_issues.fix: House rule: kill every 'Whether you're...' / 'Whether the...' construction. Rephrase as a direct statement.

The ambergris paragraph is strong but the phrase 'foul-then-fragrant' is doing a lot of work. The substance is actually odorless-to-fecal when fresh and develops its scent over years of oxidation. The binary is slightly misleading. Tighten.
This sentence is a fragment that feels like it's trying too hard to be a pull quote. It's not bad, but it's performing profundity rather than earning it. Integrate it or cut it.

research_context.venue_context:
From the 1990s, the brewery gradually reduced production. In 2006, the Neukölln facility was permanently closed, resulting in the loss of 160 jobs – a significant blow to the district. In the years that followed, the site was temporarily adopted by Berlin’s art and club scenes as a cultural venue. The Neukölln district administration advocated for its long-term use as a publicly accessible cultural site, in line with heritage protection requirements. [...] KINDL – Centre for Contemporary Art
